title: Market Day
sub: A small game about why people buy. Name your own stall at a hill market, set the prices, choose the sign, and watch the villagers decide. Then come back for Festival day and a Winter market.
description: Market Day: a small browser game by Riya Dutta. Three market days, twelve nudges and eleven villagers. Set the prices, pick the sign, and learn why each one buys or walks away.
facts: A game in the browser, nothing to download
Price tags and a chalkboard sign; a free-taste tray and prices ending in 9 at the festival; a bundle of two things in winter
A first market day, Festival day and a Winter market, where happy customers come back
What is on the counter, what each villager will pay and who comes first all change each time you play
Name it, and dress your shopkeeper: hair, a dress, kurta, lehenga or pattu, patterns, earrings and more. It’s remembered for next time and shows on your postcard
A sticker book with one sticker for each nudge you get to work, and a postcard of your day to save or share
The idea, the villagers, the drawing and the rules
One HTML file: every villager drawn in SVG, every sound and voice made in the browser

hero.alt: Riya waving beside her market stall of honey jars, apples, a woollen cap and a shawl, with a chalkboard that says Fresh this morning

sections.title: Price it, sign it, open up.
sections.note: The stall is stocked differently every visit. Tap Make it yours to name the stall and choose how you look. Tap Set prices to change the price tags, then tap the chalkboard to choose what it says. Open the stall, and change things once at lunch. At dusk, the ledger shows who bought, why, and how much more they would have paid, and you get a postcard of your day to keep. Every nudge that wins a sale earns a sticker, twelve in all. Villagers dress for the day and walk off wearing or carrying what they bought. Switch days from “Other days” in the morning; win villagers early and they come back loyal.

items.t: Most of marketing is a nudge, not a price cut. Here you can watch twelve of them at work on eleven shoppers, one at a time.
Every villager has a limit, and the right nudge stretches it. Limits shift a little every visit, so the ledger shows each reason and each limit at dusk, and the next day you price a little smarter.

tiles.d: Pip the goat pays more for the medium size when the big one costs twice as much: the decoy. Kiko the yak pays more for a cap or a cushion when something pricey sits beside it: the anchor.
Juno the monal pays more for the fruit if stock looks short. Nell the pika only buys once a crowd has, and her limit is lower. Price the fruit for one, and you may lose the other.
Wren the red panda wants to know where it was made. Tell her it is local, and keep the small one within her limit.

Lumi the marmot buys after a free taste. Bo the snow leopard cub hates to miss the last day of the season. Gus the black bear loves a price ending in 9, and eats every free taste. Pip and Wren come back loyal if you won them the day before. Everyone turns up in a party hat with a balloon.

Milo the ibex loves a bundle that costs less than its parts. Dot the snow partridge pays more when each sale gives a child a book. Tess the Tibetan fox buys a pricey shawl once the sign says it lasts ten winters. Kiko and Bo come back, and Lumi and Gus are hibernating. Everyone is bundled up in beanies, scarves and earmuffs.

paras: The rest of this site is work for clients. The Lab is for things I make because I want them to exist. This one turns the ideas I use every day into three days at a hill market, from a sunny morning to a festival to the first snow. The stock and the shoppers change every visit, so no two days play the same, but a perfect day is always possible if you get the prices and the nudges right.
